sources.title: How Damon Chen grew Testimonial.to to $400k ARR as a solo bootstrapped founder
sources.originalTitle: Building a $400k/year SaaS with Damon Chen — The Bootstrapped Founder #164
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains how a video community built to cure his own loneliness became Testimonial.to, a social proof tool at $400k ARR. He covers building in public as a growth channel, quitting only after validation, protecting family time, delegating work, and bootstrap-friendly funding and exit thinking.

principles.text: Build the first product to solve your own problem; a real business can grow out of it.
principles.quote: Lonely Dev is a community that are built to solve my own problem

principles.text: Social media exposure compounds like a snowball; word of mouth and SEO follow without extra effort.
principles.quote: most of the traffic that I got is from the social media and it's like a snowball when I get more exposure on the social media

principles.text: Quit your job only after revenue validation, and set a concrete target with a fallback to hold yourself accountable.
principles.quote: I actually quit my job when testimonial hit a thousand MRR

principles.text: Video testimonials beat text reviews because authenticity is hard to fake on camera, and trust drives conversion.
principles.quote: simply by looking at the person's face by looking at how the person talks you can immediately feel if the person is really happy or not

principles.text: Set customer expectations humanly; telling customers why you're delayed builds goodwill and lets you over-deliver.
principles.quote: I told them that hey I'm gonna take my daughter to the playground, probably be back in two hours

principles.text: Hire for the work you dislike and give contractors full ownership so they don't consume your time.
principles.quote: if I bring someone to the team I just wanna give them the full control over a project

sources.title: How Damon Chen grew Testimonial to ~$200K ARR solo: niche product, customer-led roadmap, build in public
sources.originalTitle: #22 How to get testimonials from clients | Damon Chen, Co-founder of Testimonial
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains how he quit Cisco and took Testimonial from $1K MRR to about $16K MRR as a solo founder. He covers validating with a lifetime deal, narrowing the target customer, letting customers drive the roadmap, asking for testimonials at peak excitement, and handling churn.

principles.text: Build what your customers ask for; happy customers feed acquisition.
principles.quote: my strategy my core strategy is always you know build stuff that my customers want

principles.text: As a solo developer, start with a simple niche product, not a sprawling tool you can't sell.
principles.quote: instead of you know you build a crm with uh you know hundreds of integrations how are you going to sell right and you have no marketing guys and you just by yourself

principles.text: Ask for testimonials right after a customer is delighted, not on a calendar schedule.
principles.quote: the customer will be more likely to give you a testimonial when their you know excitement is at a big level

principles.text: Don't ship one-off requests; hold a feature until multiple customers ask or it clearly affects revenue.
principles.quote: if some if a feature is asked by you know a customer which really you know has nobody else asked for it and i always put it on hold until you know more similar uh request comes in

principles.text: Check who actually pays and stays, then retarget; price-sensitive solo influencers churned, so he shifted to agencies and SMBs.
principles.quote: later that i think oh you know influencers may not be my target audience

principles.text: Building in public creates a flywheel: shipping customer-requested features gives you content, and content brings customers.
principles.quote: i keep uh getting more content to share and that brings me more uh you know customers

sources.title: Damon Chen: Testimonial.to at $4k MRR, Twitter distribution and bootstrapping from an unpaid leave
sources.originalTitle: Quit $200k job for $4k MRR side project, can he hit $100k by December?
sources.summary: Damon Chen shares how he took unpaid leave from a ~$200k Cisco job to build Testimonial.to, reaching $4k MRR with about 100 subscribers. He covers pricing tiers, Twitter-only distribution, product-led SEO via shared links and embeds, and why he took a small Earnest Capital deal for resources over money.

principles.text: Use unpaid leave instead of quitting outright: it creates urgency to earn while limiting family risk.
principles.quote: why not just i take some you know uh unpaid leave in the middle and let's see how things go

principles.text: A single well-worked channel can carry early revenue; Twitter alone drove most customers, though he flags the concentration risk.
principles.quote: i do everything on on twitter and so this is my major distribution channel so i um i actually don't have any other marketing channels

principles.text: Build virality and SEO into the product: customer-shared collection links and embeds drive backlinks, traffic and time on site.
principles.quote: if you are one of my customers and you use testimonial and you will for sure send the link to your existing customers and they will just open the testimonials link to record uh their video testimonial

principles.text: Sell a tiered plan: a mid-tier around $60/month plus an ultimate tier at $180/month that attracts bigger SaaS customers.
principles.quote: most of my big customers uh for testimonial if they send off the ultimate plan the the most expensive plan are from sas uh companies

principles.text: Take investors for resources and network, not cash: a technical solo founder needs marketing and sales help more than money.
principles.quote: i don't need any capital i don't need any money monetary you know fundings but all i need is the resources

principles.text: Give a small equity stake to an advisor a few years ahead who can hand you a hands-on marketing strategy.
principles.quote: i need the person in front of me you know three three to five years in front of me

sources.title: How Damon Chen bootstrapped Testimonial to $13k MRR after many failed side projects
sources.originalTitle: Bootstrapping Testimonial to $13k MRR after many failed products - Damon Chen, Testimonial
sources.summary: Damon pivoted his video community Indie Log into Testimonial, reusing code to ship an MVP in a week and earn $3k in 10 days via a lifetime deal. He then moved to SaaS, raised price from $10 to $60, built product-led growth hooks, and grew on Twitter by being humble.

principles.text: Build side projects for fun to avoid burnout; keep the joy of building alive.
principles.quote: side projects is really a great way for me to you know get myself distracted and not really to get burned out

principles.text: When pivoting, reuse as much existing code as possible to cut opportunity cost and ship fast.
principles.quote: if i can you know leverage what i already built reuse as much code as possible and that that that that's even better right

principles.text: Skip lengthy validation; build and launch, since paying customers are the real validation.
principles.quote: if people pay you money and that's the ultimate validation instead of people say reply your thread and say oh that's really cool

principles.text: Use a lifetime deal for early cash, then convert to subscription once demand is proven.
principles.quote: i'm a huge fan of the current business model and try to see if i can turn the product into a sas product

principles.text: Test and raise pricing aggressively; doubling price sped up revenue growth.
principles.quote: in the beginning the pricing was ten dollars per month and i just double it and until now it is 60 dollars per month

principles.text: As a solo founder, build growth hacks into the product (quotas, powered-by logo) for product-led growth.
principles.quote: i try to implement as growth hack into my product so that make my product uh fully um product led growth

sources.title: Why I diversify: running multiple bootstrapped businesses to cut risk and keep momentum
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains why he runs several bootstrapped businesses (Testimonial.to, PDF.ai, acquisitions) instead of going all in on one. Diversifying spreads risk, creates stable income, widens learning, avoids burnout and softens the exit-void after selling.

principles.text: Treat businesses like a stock portfolio: spread risk instead of relying on one business.
principles.quote: you don't put all your money in one stock you spread it out that way you know if one stock didn't go really well the others can make it up I think the same deal for business

principles.text: Bootstrappers building for their families need stable income, which multiple businesses provide better than one moonshot.
principles.quote: it is pretty important for Boost rappers because you know we mainly build our businesses for ourselves for our families so that's why we need the stable income

principles.text: Odds of a single business reaching unicorn/IPO are low, so don't plan around it.
principles.quote: I would say the chance of that happening is pretty low so let's just forget about it

principles.text: Running both B2B and B2C products lets you tap different markets and keep learning.
principles.quote: by having multiple businesses I get a chance to tap into different markets it's just fun to play in between B2B and b2c

principles.text: Staying open to new opportunities keeps you learning; each new business teaches new lessons (e.g. acquiring an AI product).
principles.quote: if you are open to any new opportunities the learning will never stop each business is a new adventure it has its own set of lessons

principles.text: Treat each new opportunity as another dart to throw; more darts raise the odds of success.
principles.quote: if every new opportunity gives me a new dart to throw I can keep collecting new darts and it will eventually increase the chance of getting the success

sources.title: Why Damon Chen started a YouTube channel after 8 years at one job and 4 years of solo bootstrapping
sources.originalTitle: Who am I and why am I starting this YouTube channel?
sources.summary: Damon Chen shares his backstory: eight years at one job, quitting in 2020 to care for his child, and learning web dev that turned into side hustles and a full-time income. He explains his reasons for starting a YouTube channel: giving back, leaving memories, and having fun without monetization pressure.

principles.text: Side hustles are best started with the safety of a full-time job, so you can enjoy building without money pressure.
principles.quote: I still have my full-time job that's the reason probably the main reason that allowed me to fully enjoying doing the S hustling without worrying too much about making money

principles.text: Build hobby projects for fun; they can accidentally grow into a full-time business that out-earns your old job.
principles.quote: I accidentally fall in love with doing some sand hustling building some hobby projects and obviously four years later my hobbies become my fulltime and I can finally make living out of it

principles.text: Give back once you have your own stories, as earlier founders did for you.
principles.quote: four years ago when I just started and I've been helped by many OG Founders Founders that I admire like kland and Rosie from uh IND hackers

principles.text: Start new channels without growth or monetization pressure; if it isn't fun, it isn't worth the time.
principles.quote: I don't want to give myself you know especially at this moment any pressure in either growing the subscribers or doing some monetization

principles.text: Stop procrastinating on things you want to do; the best time to start is now.
principles.quote: there are only two best time to plan a tree uh the first one is 20 years ago and the second best is now

principles.text: Keep the team small but efficient and enjoy the work and life.
principles.quote: I have a small but very efficient team and for me I'm just enjoying my work in life at the moment

sources.title: How Damon Chen went from a lonely-dev side project to Testimonial and full time
sources.originalTitle: From Side Project to Full Time with Damon Chen and Michael Rouveure (Software Social transcript)
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains how he pivoted a video community (lonely.dev) into Testimonial by reusing most of the code, launched fast on Product Hunt with a lifetime deal, and quit his Cisco job in public at $1K MRR. He also covers why he took calm fund money as a solo founder and how to tell if money or product-market fit is your blocker.

principles.text: Pivot a project into a new product by reusing code you already shipped, to cut opportunity and time cost.
principles.quote: The best use case for me is to just reuse the code that I previously shipped to lonely dev and try to see if I can pivot into a standalone product.

principles.text: Build what solves your own selling problem: social proof is a universal need for indie hackers.
principles.quote: how can I sell the product? How can I get the social proof and prove that potential buyers that, hey, this is the legit and you can buy it.

principles.text: Launch fast: ship an MVP in about a week, launch on Product Hunt the next day, and use a lifetime deal for early cash.
principles.quote: I can quickly build the MVP within a week. I launch it, I directly launch it, after the MVP is done, the next day I launched it on product hunt.

principles.text: Early revenue is the strongest validation and motivation.
principles.quote: I would say the, uh, stripe notification is the thing about, you know, energized me during the first few launch days.

principles.text: Set a public revenue milestone to quit your job and agree the downside with your family up front.
principles.quote: if I can reach a 1000 MRR, I'm going to quit, quit my job in public.

principles.text: Identify what actually blocks you from going full time: if it is money, take funding; if it is product-market fit, validate first.
principles.quote: you got to know what is the thing that blocks you from really quitting our job? You know, I mean, if it is money, take the money.

sources.title: Damon Chen: From Cisco engineer to $1.3M ARR across Testimonial and PDF.ai
sources.originalTitle: Damon Chen: From Engineer to Indie Hacker Making $1,300,000 ARR (Behind the Craft Q&A)
sources.summary: Damon Chen recounts leaving Cisco after four failed side projects to build Testimonial to $800K+ ARR alone, then PDF.ai to $500K+. The free portion covers launching on Product Hunt, product-led growth loops, an affiliate program, buying a typo domain, and negotiating the risk with his wife. The PDF.ai growth channels are paywalled.

principles.text: Reuse existing code and ship fast: a failed project's codebase can become the next product.
principles.quote: It used about 80% of the same code as Indielog. I just added a landing page and Stripe payments before launching it on Product Hunt

principles.text: Launch with lifetime deals to get early cash and validation before moving to subscriptions.
principles.quote: I was selling lifetime access for $199. I sold 30 deals and generated $6K in revenue in the first two weeks.

principles.text: Engineers who dislike marketing can lean on product-led growth: let the product's output carry a branded link back to signup.
principles.quote: I’m an engineer who doesn’t know much about marketing or sales. Instead, I focused on product-led growth.

principles.text: A branded badge on free output is both a growth loop and an upgrade incentive.
principles.quote: The testimonial logo also incentivized people to upgrade to the paid plan to remove it.

principles.text: A generous recurring-commission affiliate program can drive a meaningful share of revenue.
principles.quote: gives anyone who signs up a paid customer 30% commission every month. The customer also gets 15% off for the first year. This program contributes about 10-15% of our total revenue.

principles.text: Buying the look-alike domain people mistakenly visit can pay back: $35K on testimonial.io returned $80K lifetime.
principles.quote: I realized that many people mistakenly visited testimonial.io instead of testimonial.to. So I spent $35,000 to buy the .io domain.

sources.title: How Damon Chen acquired PDF.ai and grew it past $50K MRR
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains how he bought a weekend-built AI project, rebranded it to PDF.ai, validated demand with a $99 lifetime deal, and grew it mostly through organic search thanks to an exact-match domain. He also shares what he would do differently: influencer marketing and partnerships.

principles.text: Buy a validated, hyped weekend project instead of starting from zero.
principles.quote: It creates some hype when being announced on social media. It's kind of like validation to me. When the project was listed for sale, it grabbed my attention, and eventually I acquired it.

principles.text: Use a lifetime deal to test willingness to pay and fund the build.
principles.quote: I offered a lifetime deal at $99. With over 300 adopters within a 3-month campaign, it provided enough validation for the monetization aspect and strong financial support to invest more effort into growing PDF.ai.

principles.text: Reinvest early revenue into a full-time engineer.
principles.quote: I used the revenue from the LTD to hire a full-time engineer to work on it.

principles.text: A relevant, exact-match domain name is a top SEO and marketing asset.
principles.quote: Top marketing effort is the relevant domain name. The domain name explicitly tells Google what we do, and our product is exactly like the domain says.

principles.text: A good domain helps you compete for difficult keywords early.
principles.quote: So picking a good, relevant domain for your business will give you a head start in competing for some difficult keywords.

principles.text: Don't rely only on shipping features and waiting for virality; add influencer and partnership channels.
principles.quote: If I were to do it differently, I would explore more marketing channels, collaborate with influencers in their respective spaces

sources.title: How Damon Chen built IndieLog: a video-first indie hacker community born from his own loneliness
sources.originalTitle: Creator Interview with Damon Chen (Michael Brooks)
sources.summary: Damon Chen explains how he built IndieLog (a vlog community for indie hackers) to solve his own remote-work isolation, and how a launch on Indie Hackers then Product Hunt plus daily presence seeded it. He also covers features designed to drive member activity and his plan to add gamification.

principles.text: Build products from a problem you personally have; the idea came from his own isolation while working from home.
principles.quote: the idea was coming from my own problem. Starting from this March, I began to work from home because of the lockdown.

principles.text: Differentiate by being more human than existing options instead of cloning another text forum.
principles.quote: I don’t want to create another one. I want to create something a little more human where people can have more personalized interactions.

principles.text: Launch in the community where your target users already gather; the Indie Hackers launch produced uploads within a day.
principles.quote: I launched indielog on Indiehackers community, one day later, I got several new video uploads.

principles.text: Follow the community launch with Product Hunt for extra traffic, then stay consistent and active rather than over-promoting.
principles.quote: After that, I didn’t do too much promotion, but I try to be consistent to update my work on Indielog almost every day and be very active to interact with other members in our community.

principles.text: Ship features whose common goal is to drive member contribution (topics lower the blank-page barrier, products tie updates to progress).
principles.quote: The common goal of all these things is to motivate members to do more video updates.

principles.text: A small community can be a feature, not a flaw, when closeness is the value.
principles.quote: we are still very small, we have less than 200 members, but to me, it’s good to be small as well. It like a friend circle I created all around the world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains how a video community built to cure his own loneliness became Testimonial.to, a social proof tool at $400k ARR. He covers building in public as a growth channel, quitting only after validation, protecting family time, delegating work, and bootstrap-friendly funding and exit thinking.

chunks.heading: Origin of testimonial.to: from Lonely Dev to Indie Log to video testimonials
chunks.text:
- Damon built Lonely Dev in early 2020 to solve his own loneliness. He was a Cisco employee in the Bay Area forced to work from home, and he missed coffee chats with coworkers.
- He did not want another text-based community like Indie Hackers or a subreddit. He built a video-focused community where members post video updates and ask for help on camera.
- He never planned to monetize it. He had a paycheck, and the community was only tens to a few hundred active members. As sole moderator, 20 to 30 video updates a day was plenty to watch and reply to.
- Community members said "Lonely Dev" sounded inactive, so he renamed it Indie Log. He kept "Indie" from Indie Hackers for brand recognition and paired it with "log" for vlogging.
- He built several other products in 2020 that made no money. As an engineer looking for a shortcut, he wanted to add social proof to landing pages, but text reviews did not appeal to him.
- Seeing video reviews from Shopify developers on a Shopify developer website made him think video testimonials could plug into his video-focused work. He pivoted the product from Lonely Dev into testimonial.to.

chunks.heading: Why video testimonials and social proof work
chunks.text:
- Damon's view: "people buy from people." A visitor who has never heard of a product or seen anyone vouch for it is less likely to convert.
- He sees text reviews as easy to fake and not very attractive. He describes them as short, templated lines like "great product, highly recommended" with five stars, often with stock-photo avatars.
- Fake text reviews can hurt a business. Video is a different technology: even if the person says nothing, you can tell from their face and how they talk whether they are really happy.
- He says video is the format that no other kind of review can compete with on authenticity.
- He built the product around connecting with real people, a thread that runs back to Lonely Dev.
- testimonial.to lets you collect testimonials and import reviews from third-party sites (e.g. Twitter, Amazon), and positions itself as a one-stop shop to manage social proof across the internet in one "wall of love."

chunks.heading: Growth: from $1k MRR to $400k ARR through building in public
chunks.text:
- At the time of the interview (Nov 2022), testimonial.to had reached $400k ARR. Damon described it as growing almost double-digit percent month over month, and had been at about $4k MRR a year to a year and a half earlier.
- Most of his traffic comes from social media. He calls it a snowball: more exposure leads to SEO and word of mouth arriving organically without extra work.
- The product markets itself in a self-referential way, since a testimonial tool can be used to show testimonials about itself.
- He expected to reach $1M ARR around the following year. He called $1M a magic number many bootstrappers aim for.
- His team was just him plus a marketing hire he made the week before the interview.

chunks.heading: Quitting the job: the $100k ARR promise and what he would advise
chunks.text:
- Damon did not quit with zero revenue. He quit his job when testimonial.to hit $1,000 MRR.
- He showed his wife his MRR chart to project growth, and promised to reach $100k ARR within nine months. If he failed, he would go back and find a job. If he made it, he would stick with it. He hit $100k ARR after nine months.
- He says he would not suggest anyone quit without validation. His advice is to be financially prepared (some revenue validation) and mentally prepared.
- His safety net was being a software engineer in the Bay Area, where he could always get a job again. Before the pandemic he had interviewed with big tech companies but found the interview prep (months of coding practice) boring. He saw that a new employer would mostly mean the same work for higher pay.
- A worst case of losing six months of paycheck seemed acceptable to him.
- The trigger was the pandemic: his daughter (born 2018) was not in daycare, his wife worked at a startup with growing demands, and one of them needed to take on care. He chose to do side hustles and build products.

chunks.heading: Running a business with a young child and setting expectations
chunks.text:
- Early on, with an immature product and a lot of customer feedback, he cared for his one-and-a-half-year-old daughter during the day and worked at night, burning "midnight oil" to fix things and implement features.
- He says he told customers things like "I have to take my daughter to the playground, can I reply in an hour or two?" Customers understood, and some knew him from Twitter.
- He prioritizes family over instant support. He says he sacrificed a paycheck for precious family time, so it makes no sense to sacrifice that time for customers. Losing a few customers is recoverable; a toddler period only happens once.
- His technique is to set the expectation low and beat it: he tells customers a reply will come by end of day, then usually replies within 30 minutes to an hour, so they get responses faster than expected.
- Damon says it is not good to run a one-man business, partly because if he is with his kids the business is paused and nobody else can move the needle.
- He and his wife had a second child in June 2022, which was one reason to bring on help.

chunks.heading: Hiring and delegation philosophy
chunks.text:
- Damon hired a marketing person (about a week before the interview) because he does not feel he handles marketing and sales well. He does not want to spend time on repetitive, human-effort work like cold outreach.
- Reasons it was the right time: the business was growing and profitable, the new baby, and a single-point-of-failure problem. The hire should complement his skills by handling marketing and sales.
- He has no plans to grow the engineering side. He does not want to manage engineers.
- When he does work with others, he wants to be the manager he wished he'd had. He gives people full control over a project.
- He uses Upwork freelancers and contractors for small, defined projects. He gives ideas and mockups, and wants them to deliver a working version without constant questions.
- He dislikes contractors who ask for constant feedback and charge a low rate. His example: someone at $50/hour who also costs him several hours a day effectively costs about $100/hour once his own time is counted.
- He sometimes hires more than one person on the same project to compare results. He can always check the GitHub repo but does not want questions on small details.

chunks.heading: Exit thinking and what "life-changing money" means in the Bay Area
chunks.text:
- Damon had no exit plan. He noted that a founder friend (Jon Yongfook) mentioned he could sell Banner Bear at about 5x ARR, roughly $2M, but chose not to.
- For Damon, $2M is good money but not life-changing in the Bay Area. Software engineers there earn $200k to $300k per year, and housing costs millions.
- His own benchmark: if he worked at a big tech company at $300k and could then not work for 20 years, that is about $6M. He treats a figure in the several-millions range as life-changing.
- A team also argues for a larger exit so the team benefits.
- He relayed advice from an unnamed founder who sold his business (a "live training zone" business): think about exit now, shop around, and negotiate well, since a poor exit negotiation can cost several million dollars.
- That founder reportedly got a strong offer by presenting a valuation based on VC-style numbers to private equity and naming the price he would sell at.

chunks.heading: Funding: Calm Fund, and bootstrapper-friendly options
chunks.text:
- testimonial.to took a small investment from Calm Fund (formerly Earnest Capital) when it was close to $2,000 MRR. Damon described the equity given as a single digit percentage.
- What he valued was the community of portfolio founders, many doing several million dollars in revenue. He says they give practical, approachable advice rather than random YouTube advice. He says he "paid equity to get a ticket into the community."
- He plans to stay bootstrapped for further funding.
- He mentioned non-dilutive options like Pipe, where you get annual revenue upfront in exchange for giving a discount to the funder, which he sees as a way to get capital without giving up equity. He also pointed to Founderpath as another such option.
- His rationale: the capital is used for the team, and these options are data-driven and tied to revenue, not to disrupting a market.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains how he quit Cisco and took Testimonial from $1K MRR to about $16K MRR as a solo founder. He covers validating with a lifetime deal, narrowing the target customer, letting customers drive the roadmap, asking for testimonials at peak excitement, and handling churn.

chunks.heading: Starting from a 1k MRR side project: quitting the job and the first-year goal
chunks.text:
- Damon left Cisco in May 2021, about 4-5 months after launching Testimonial. He had been a software engineer for 8 years.
- Trigger: during Covid his daughter (1.5-2 years old) stayed home 24/7 and his wife also worked from home. He was under heavy pressure juggling standups for his day job and childcare, and felt his day-job output was suffering.
- He decided family was the top priority: "it's only once for a dad to spend more time with her in her young age."
- Testimonial had just hit $1,000 MRR in April, which he took as the signal to double down and give up the engineering salary.
- He publicly tweeted a commitment to his wife: reach $100k ARR by the end of year one, or go back to a software engineering job. He notes getting hired in Silicon Valley would not be hard, so the downside felt manageable.
- Result at the time of the interview (June 2022): about $16k MRR, nearly $200k ARR, as a solo founder with no employees.
- His reasoning for staying committed: he had spent years dedicated to a single employer, so he should give his own project the same long-term consistency.

chunks.heading: How Testimonial grew out of Lonely.dev and early validation
chunks.text:
- Damon's first product was Lonely.dev, a video-first community for makers and indie hackers, where members record short video updates and ask for help. He built it during Covid when he felt isolated working from home.
- Making videos for that community pushed him to talk on camera and expose himself publicly, and he then moved to Twitter for broader reach.
- Testimonial was a pivot: Lonely.dev already had video recording, sharing, hosting and streaming, so he reused much of the code. He launched the MVP in about two weeks.
- The idea came from his own pain: he built side projects with no reviews, then saw a section of video testimonials on a Shopify page and thought of productizing the video part.
- He launched with a lifetime deal at $199 and sold roughly 20 copies, about $3-4k in two weeks, which validated demand.
- Based on a Product Hunt comment suggesting a subscription model, he switched to subscriptions only and has focused on recurring revenue since.

chunks.heading: Build in public as an accidental flywheel
chunks.text:
- He did not plan to build in public. He started tweeting to document his journey and the audience grew beyond what he expected. His first customers came from Twitter.
- His core strategy: "build stuff that my customers want."
- Flywheel as he describes it: early customers give feedback, he ships the requested features, happy customers recommend the product, and each shipped feature gives him more content to share publicly, which brings more customers.
- Example: the "Wall of Love" (embeddable testimonial display) was suggested by early customers. The first version only let customers collect videos, with no way to distribute them.
- As a developer new to marketing, he leaned on his existing strength (shipping product) rather than trying to become a marketing guru.

chunks.heading: Advice for developers who don't want to do marketing
chunks.text:
- Building a business is not just launching a product. A product launch does not bring millions of customers automatically; marketing and sales have to be learned.
- Commit to at least one to two years, otherwise it stays a hobby that only builds technical skill.
- Start with a niche audience and a simple product for a specific need. A clear value proposition and an easy-to-use product are easier to sell.
- His warning: with a CRM with hundreds of integrations and no marketing help, "how are you going to sell?"
- Validate the market with a simple tool, then let customers determine the features instead of building what you fantasize is cool and finding months later that nobody wants it.
- Listen to people who actually have the problem and are waiting for someone to solve it.

chunks.heading: Finding the right customer segment and handling churn
chunks.text:
- His initial assumption was that Testimonial would suit influencers collecting testimonials from fans. It didn't work: influencers already have tons of social proof and reputation, they are solo and price-sensitive, and at $20-30 per month they churned quickly if the product didn't justify the cost.
- He dug through who had actually subscribed and found agencies and marketing departments in sales-oriented companies. They paid and stayed longer, so he shifted his target to SMBs.
- Churn: it was historically around 2-3% monthly, and spiked to 5% the previous month.
- Collecting feedback showed customers called it too expensive, and most churners were very small businesses. Checking usage showed churners had collected few videos, while retained customers received many videos and got marketing assets from them.
- His focus: help customers collect more testimonials so they get value.
- On fixing churn, he prefers to look forward: ship a better product and more features rather than chase churned users, especially as a one-person business. Some churned users reactivate monthly after he ships features they wanted.
- He rejects paid or incentivized reviews: testimonials "should be candid."

chunks.heading: How to get testimonials from customers
chunks.text:
- Ask at the moment of peak excitement. When a customer requests a feature and he ships it, he contacts them directly for feedback. If they say they love it, he asks for a testimonial then, because "the customer will be more likely to give you a testimonial when their excitement is at a big level."
- He does not wait a month after signup and cold-ask. He goes after each happy customer individually and only asks those who feel good about the product. A good product comes first.
- Automation he sees customers using: Zapier triggers from review platforms such as Trustpilot or Google. When a customer leaves a five-star text review, an email is triggered asking them for a video testimonial.
- Large companies he observes embed a testimonial link in marketing campaign emails whenever they launch a new product line, sending to millions of users, which shows up as traffic spikes on his monitoring.
- Other use case he noticed: a company running a testimonial campaign to collect video best wishes from employees for a retiring colleague in a remote team.

chunks.heading: Why testimonials are an ongoing asset
chunks.text:
- Embedded Testimonial widgets carry "Powered by" branding, which gives him backlinks and social proof. A business embedding 10 videos shows visitors that others collected them with his tool, even if that customer later churns.
- Marketing teams need fresh testimonials for paid campaigns, since reusing one person repeatedly gets stale.
- Video testimonials on landing pages also build the trust that supports conversion.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing as a solo founder and running on gut
chunks.text:
- Early days were chaotic: he tended to ship any request within hours and exhausted himself, then built a large backlog.
- His prioritization rules now:
  - If only one customer asks for a feature, put it on hold, note the request, tell the customer, and wait for more similar requests.
  - Prioritize by number of requests.
  - Prioritize features with revenue impact, such as paid-plan features that make people upgrade.
  - Follow his gut and vision for where Testimonial should go.
- On data vs gut: with a small customer base, he argues gut matters more. If it doesn't work out, "I'm a one-man business, I can pivot pretty fast," and it becomes a lesson.
- His days run late (bed around midnight or 1am) because of the workload.

chunks.heading: Mindset and influences
chunks.text:
- Book recommendation: The Intelligent Investor by Benjamin Graham. It moved him from day trading to long-term value investing (he cites his Tesla stock gains). He applies the same idea to business: find an underserved niche, build a better solution, and be patient for several years.
- Founder inspiration: Pieter Levels, whose one-person business and "12 startups in 12 months" showed him he didn't have to climb a corporate engineering ladder.
- To regain energy in tough times, he spends time with his daughter and tries to look at problems the way she does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen shares how he took unpaid leave from a ~$200k Cisco job to build Testimonial.to, reaching $4k MRR with about 100 subscribers. He covers pricing tiers, Twitter-only distribution, product-led SEO via shared links and embeds, and why he took a small Earnest Capital deal for resources over money.

chunks.heading: Product and pricing: Testimonial.to at roughly $4k MRR
chunks.text:
- Damon builds Testimonial.to, a tool for collecting video (and text) testimonials. It was his pivot after several earlier products, mostly video-related; he reused front-end and UI work from those, so he spent $0 on Upwork freelancers for Testimonial.
- Pricing he states: $60/month or $80/year on the standard paid plan, and an "ultimate" plan at $180/month or $1,440/year. His biggest customers, the ones on the ultimate plan, are SaaS companies.
- Customer mix: e-commerce merchants, product makers, podcasters and SaaS founders. Anyone with customers who might vouch for them is a target.
- Metrics he shared in June 2021 (first time publicly): a bit over 100 active paying subscribers, and MRR just crossed $4,000 (a bit under $4k the month before). Roughly $50k ARR.
- New subscribers: 30 net-new active subscribers the prior month, 11 so far in the current month (early June).

chunks.heading: Quitting a $200k job by taking unpaid leave
chunks.text:
- Damon worked at Cisco with a total package close to $200,000 a year (about $15-16k/month).
- Rather than quit outright, he took unpaid personal leave in 2020. He keeps medical coverage, which matters because he has a two-year-old daughter.
- His reasoning: a lower-risk way to test whether Testimonial takes off before resigning. Losing the paycheck created the urgency to make money that he lacked while collecting biweekly pay.
- He launched Testimonial.to right before Christmas 2020.
- Looking back, he wishes at 20 he had known about side projects and passive income instead of only chasing a full-time job at his "dream company" (Cisco).

chunks.heading: Growth goal and distribution channels
chunks.text:
- His stated goal is $100k by end of year, which he calls realistic given the current trajectory. He says he doesn't want to set expectations so high that missing them is demoralizing.
- Distribution: nearly all customers come from Twitter. He runs no cold email, no outbound and no paid ads.
- He sees Twitter as both a strength and a single point of failure, and says LinkedIn is the next big channel, especially for SaaS buyers on the ultimate plan.
- Being a solo bootstrapper with limited time is why he hasn't diversified yet. He plans to reinvest recurring revenue into other channels over time.

chunks.heading: Product-led SEO: ranking for "testimonial" without writing content
chunks.text:
- Damon tweeted in June 2021 that Testimonial.to was ranking high on Google for the keyword "testimonial", ahead of HubSpot.
- He wrote no dedicated testimonial blog content. His explanation is that the product generates traffic by itself:
  - Customers send a link to their own customers to record a video or text testimonial, which drives visitors to the Testimonial.to site.
  - Customers embed collected testimonials on their own websites, which creates backlinks.
- On why the site ranks, Damon says he is "not a SEO guy" and isn't sure what exactly qualifies.

chunks.heading: Earnest Capital: small investment for resources, not cash
chunks.text:
- Damon took a small investment from Earnest Capital (under $100k, exact number not disclosed) in exchange for a little equity. He still owns the vast majority of the company.
- Why: he didn't need money. He's a technical solo founder, "totally newbie" at marketing and sales, and wanted Earnest's pool of successful founders, warm intros and resources. He says Earnest has emailed its list for him, which drove new customers.
- His explanation of how Earnest's deal works: they invest an amount for a percentage of equity, and as the company generates revenue it returns a multiple (he cites 3x) of the investment to buy back equity, leaving Earnest a small residual stake (he says around 2%). His illustrative numbers ($100k, 6%, 3x) were loose, so treat them as an example of the shape, not terms.
- On extra money: no plans to raise more. He'd use Upwork freelancers for any big feature work, and will re-evaluate after a marketing strategy and feature roadmap are in place.

chunks.heading: Using an equity-compensated advisor instead of a co-founder
chunks.text:
- He considered a co-founder but hasn't found one. Instead he recently brought on an advisor he met on Twitter, Darren Westall, and gave him equity.
- Darren founded Pager.co, a platform for marketing agencies and recruiters, described by Damon as a multi-million dollar business in England.
- The arrangement: a weekly or biweekly meeting where Darren lays out a marketing strategy.
- Why he picked him: Damon wants someone only a few years ahead of him, who can give hands-on, executable advice, rather than a founder of a Nasdaq-listed company giving high-level advice. He believes he can take Testimonial to multi-million dollars in 3-5 years.

chunks.heading: Tools and influences
chunks.text:
- Video hosting and processing: Mux, which he uses for all his video-related products.
- Reading: "Zero to Sold" by Arvid Kahl, and he had bought Arvid's second book, "The Embedded Entrepreneur".
- Founder he follows: Nick Castle (Hebrew sleep.so), who went from gas station worker to a successful entrepreneur; sleep.so is a platform for developers to sell courses.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon pivoted his video community Indie Log into Testimonial, reusing code to ship an MVP in a week and earn $3k in 10 days via a lifetime deal. He then moved to SaaS, raised price from $10 to $60, built product-led growth hooks, and grew on Twitter by being humble.

chunks.heading: Early path: side projects built for fun while employed at Cisco
chunks.text:
- Damon worked at Cisco for eight years before going full-time as an indie hacker.
- He built Indie Log (originally "Lonely Dev") at the start of the pandemic. Working remotely made him lonely, and Indie Hackers was text-only, so he wanted a warmer, video-based community where people post short clips of what they did that day.
- He then built Howdy Influencer, Backlogs and other projects. He treats these as side projects to reset his mind and avoid burnout: "just want to get distractions so that I won't get burned out from a single project."
- None made revenue. He kept his bi-weekly Cisco paycheck, so there was no pressure, and he didn't want to charge his Indie Log community members, who were friends.
- Earlier still he tried becoming an eBay or Shopify merchant and a photographer, just to make money. Entrepreneurship was always on his mind.
- He credits Peter Levels' "12 startups in 12 months" as the inspiration for building many projects before launching Testimonial.
- His advice: keep the fun in building, not only when a product earns revenue.

chunks.heading: Pivoting Indie Log into Testimonial and making $3k in 10 days
chunks.text:
- Testimonial was a direct pivot from Indie Log. The video upload, hosting and streaming core already existed.
- The moment he decided to quit his job, he felt pressure to make money, at least be "ramen profitable". He also didn't want to push so hard that he burned out.
- His rule: reuse as much existing code as possible so a failure costs little opportunity time.
- He has no marketing or sales team, so he looked for a product that sells itself. Social proof came to mind: help makers and business owners collect video testimonials and embed them on their websites.
- He built the MVP in about a week and launched on Product Hunt in December 2020.
- It made about $3k in the first 10 days, mostly from a lifetime deal. It reached roughly $13k MRR by the time of this interview (April 2022).

chunks.heading: Skipping validation: build it and let payment validate
chunks.text:
- On Testimonial, Damon did not spend time on idea validation.
- His reasoning: the time spent validating is about the time it takes to build, and paying customers are the only real validation.
- On people replying "cool idea, I'd buy": "in the end they will never come back and they will never be becoming a customer."
- This works best when the MVP can be built in about a week and much of the code is reused.

chunks.heading: From lifetime deal to subscription SaaS
chunks.text:
- The first 10 days were mostly lifetime-deal sales. Seeing real demand, Damon decided he was "a huge fan of the current business model" (recurring revenue) and turned Testimonial into a SaaS.
- He announced that in three days the lifetime deal would end and the product would be subscription-only. The announcement itself brought in a couple thousand dollars more.
- After that he focused only on subscriptions.

chunks.heading: Pricing: starting at $10 and doubling up to $60/month
chunks.text:
- He tested pricing a lot. Testimonial started at $10/month, then he doubled it, and it reached $60/month.
- He says raising the price quite a lot "really helps speed up revenue growth."

chunks.heading: Product-led growth built into the product
chunks.text:
- As a solo founder he can't spend time on manual work like cold outreach, so he builds growth into the product and automates as much as possible to focus on building.
- Free tier limits are the upgrade trigger: free users can collect two videos; when they collect a third they must upgrade to see it.
- Embedded widgets carry a "powered by Testimonial" logo on the free plan, which acts as distribution.
- Beyond that he iterates quickly on real user feedback and does marketing by building in public on Twitter.

chunks.heading: Side products and acquiring Support Man
chunks.text:
- Embed.so brings in about $150 MRR; Channel.so has made no revenue yet. Both reuse code from Indie Log and Testimonial.
- He doesn't spend much time on them. His rule: he only works on a side project if Testimonial also benefits, since they are about 2% of his total revenue.
- He acquired Support Man, an Intercom app by Noah Bragg that syncs low-star Intercom reviews to a Slack channel so support can follow up with angry customers.
- The logic is complementary: Testimonial captures happy customers (a 4-5 star review is a good moment to ask for a testimonial), while Support Man catches unhappy ones. Intercom integration is a big ecosystem opportunity.
- The deal: Damon tweeted that he wanted to buy it, the founder was already in his Slack, asked for something over $30k, and they settled at $20k. It closed in under two hours because he already knew and trusted the seller.

chunks.heading: Twitter growth: be genuine, humble and an underdog
chunks.text:
- He grew from about 1,000 followers in the Indie Log days to roughly 27,000, almost 30,000, in about a year.
- His strategy: "be genuine, be humble and be an underdog." He calls himself "just a mediocre software engineer" who spent eight years at Cisco without being promoted to tech lead.
- He doesn't try to teach. He shares his own story so it resonates with others.
- Recommendations: the book *Getaway* by Andrew Gastaki (as transcribed), and Peter Levels as his all-time favorite indie hacker.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains why he runs several bootstrapped businesses (Testimonial.to, PDF.ai, acquisitions) instead of going all in on one. Diversifying spreads risk, creates stable income, widens learning, avoids burnout and softens the exit-void after selling.

chunks.heading: Why Damon diversifies across multiple businesses
chunks.text:
Damon Chen, a bootstrapper since early 2020, runs a portfolio of businesses rather than one. Two flagship projects are testimonial.to and pdf.ai, plus others he built and others he acquired.

- His stated view: diversifying is "an important strategy" that reduces risk and maximizes opportunities.
- He acknowledges the "go all in, avoid distractions" camp has a point, but says diversification is the approach that has worked for him.
- Portfolio overview lives at damon.vc.

chunks.heading: Spreading risk and stabilizing income
chunks.text:
- Damon compares it to investing: you don't put all your money in one stock, so a loss in one is covered by others. He applies the same logic to business.
- Relying on one business is "much riskier," especially for bootstrappers, who mainly build for themselves and their families and therefore need stable income.
- He argues the "go all in and reach unicorn/IPO in 5 to 10 years" outcome has a pretty low chance of happening, so he sets it aside.
- With several businesses, he is not solely dependent on any one. If one underperforms, others make up for it, giving a more stable income stream.
- His conclusion: "the safest and the easiest way is just to build multiple businesses."

chunks.heading: Playing in different markets: B2B and B2C
chunks.text:
- Owning several businesses lets him "dip my toes into various ponds."
- Testimonial.to is B2B: it helps business owners collect, manage and distribute testimonials efficiently.
- PDF.ai is B2C: individual consumers use AI to chat with PDF files.
- He says it is simply fun to play in both B2B and B2C.

chunks.heading: Continuous learning from each new business
chunks.text:
- Each business is "a new adventure" with its own lessons, as long as you stay open to new opportunities.
- Example: he started out building Testimonial.to with little exposure to AI. After the ChatGPT buzz, he got into PDF.ai, which he acquired rather than built from scratch.
- Working on it exposed him to OpenAI's tools and the very fast pace of AI development, keeping him up to date.
- He compares it to "playing a game that's constantly leveling up."

chunks.heading: Freedom as a solo bootstrapped founder
chunks.text:
- As a solo founder with no VC, he has no commitment forcing him to do only one thing, so he can explore freely.
- He describes his DNA as "the creator": when he sees something interesting he gets hyped and wants to try it.
- Focusing on a single project would mean missing opportunities.
- His framing: every new opportunity is a new dart to throw. Keep collecting darts and the chance of eventual success rises.
- He grabs new opportunities as they come up.

chunks.heading: Avoiding burnout and keeping the work engaging
chunks.text:
- Diversifying makes the journey less boring and more exciting, and lowers the chance of burnout.
- He has seen many founders desperate to grow one business, hit a plateau or decline, and get discouraged after putting in huge effort without matching reward. That can lead to giving up or burnout.
- With multiple businesses the workload balances out: if one feels overwhelming, he can work on another, which takes load off and keeps the whole system balanced.

chunks.heading: Easier exits: avoiding the "now what?" void
chunks.text:
- Damon notes many successful founders feel lost after selling their one and only business ("that is their baby"), asking "what's next, what am I going to do?"
- Because he runs several, selling one is not a problem: he can move his extra bandwidth to the businesses he still runs, so he doesn't expect to fall into that void.
- He says this benefit hasn't applied yet but will help in the future if he sells a business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen shares his backstory: eight years at one job, quitting in 2020 to care for his child, and learning web dev that turned into side hustles and a full-time income. He explains his reasons for starting a YouTube channel: giving back, leaving memories, and having fun without monetization pressure.

chunks.heading: Why Damon started building: from an 8-year corporate job to side hustles
chunks.text:
- Damon spent 8 years at his original software engineering job (Cisco, going by the mugs and t-shirts he mentions) and never switched, unlike most Silicon Valley engineers who change jobs every 2 to 3 years for a raise.
- He didn't stay by choice: he applied elsewhere and "got all rejected." He expected to stay until retirement.
- The turning point was childcare. His first kid was born in 2018, and in 2020 (as she was about to start daycare) Covid hit. He and his wife either had to risk daycare or have one of them quit to care for her at home. He quit.
- While at home he learned web development on Udemy during her naps and late evenings. His original goal was only to pick up a modern stack to land a better job at a new company.
- Instead he "accidentally fell in love" with side hustling and building hobby projects.

chunks.heading: Outcome: hobby projects became a full-time business
chunks.text:
- Four years after starting (as of early 2024), his hobbies became his full-time work, and he can make a living from it.
- Income is now "even better" than his old job.
- He is the founder of:
  - a SaaS product that helps business owners collect, manage and distribute testimonials
  - PDF AI, an AI product that lets users chat with PDF documents
  - other small businesses
- He runs a small but "very efficient" team.

chunks.heading: Why side hustling worked: no money pressure
chunks.text:
- He recalls that when he started hustling he still had his full-time job, which is "probably the main reason" he could fully enjoy building without worrying about making money.
- He applies the same principle to his YouTube channel: no pressure to grow subscribers or monetize, because those are unnecessary at this stage.
- His rule: "If there's no fun there's no point in doing it."

chunks.heading: Learning from and giving back to the indie community
chunks.text:
- When he started four years earlier, he was helped by founders he admires: Arvid Kahl and Rosie (Indie Hackers), Ling Tha (key values), and Peter Levels (Nomad List).
- Having been "in the arena" for four years, he feels he has his own stories to share and wants to give back the way they helped him.
- He positions the channel as a personal record of his ups and downs, in the spirit of Matt Damon planting potatoes on Mars in *The Martian*, which he hopes might also help or inspire others.

chunks.heading: Why a YouTube channel (not a newsletter), and why now
chunks.text:
- **Memories:** He wants to leave something for his kids to look back on, to see how their dad looked and talked 20 or 30 years later. He tweets nearly every day, but argues nobody will read a Twitter feed "word by word," whereas video is "more vivid."
- **Fun and new experience:** Making videos is a different experience from quickly typing tweets, and a way to step out of his comfort zone.
- **Giving back:** Sharing the story and lessons from his own journey.
- He had procrastinated on starting a channel for a long time, always telling himself he would start.
- What finally pushed him was a quote from Ali Abdaal on a Chinese saying: the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, and the second best time is now. His takeaway is to start now and let hindsight explain why it was the right time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains how he pivoted a video community (lonely.dev) into Testimonial by reusing most of the code, launched fast on Product Hunt with a lifetime deal, and quit his Cisco job in public at $1K MRR. He also covers why he took calm fund money as a solo founder and how to tell if money or product-market fit is your blocker.

chunks.heading: Damon's path from employee side projects to a bootstrapped full-time SaaS
chunks.text:
- Damon worked at Cisco for eight years in Silicon Valley. When the pandemic hit in early 2020 and Cisco went remote, he felt lonely working from home.
- He read the Indie Hackers community but felt disconnected because it was all text. So he built a video-focused community, lonely.dev, "just for fun."
- He kept the day job while building. In late 2020 the pandemic dragged on, his daughter was about one and a half, and the family wanted to keep her out of daycare for safety. He took a six-month unpaid leave.
- The unpaid leave removed his paycheck, which created financial pressure. That pushed him to turn what he had already built into a standalone product.
- His rule: building a brand new product has big opportunity and time costs, so reuse as much existing code as possible.
- He had built several side projects, and every one shared the same problem: how to get social proof so buyers trust you. He saw video testimonials on a Shopify page and decided to build a video testimonial product.

chunks.heading: Building Testimonial from lonely.dev and launching without validation
chunks.text:
- Damon reused roughly 80-90% of the lonely.dev code for Testimonial (the video recording and streaming features he had already shipped).
- He built the MVP in about a week and did not validate the idea beforehand. He says the launch results were a surprise.
- He launched on Product Hunt the next day after finishing the MVP, right before Christmas 2020.
- He sold a lifetime deal: 10 or 20 copies in the first two weeks, which brought in about $5,000 in revenue.
- The launch revenue was a strong validation that "it probably can be a thing."
- He says the Stripe notifications "energized" him during the first launch days.
- Context for the launch: his wife was sick (possible COVID) and isolated in the bedroom, so he was cooking and caring for his daughter alone. He only worked during her nap time and in the evenings after bedtime.
- His daily routine while on leave: play with his daughter, read books and play Lego during the day, and work on Testimonial during naps and after bedtime.

chunks.heading: Quitting in public and the risk framework
chunks.text:
- Before quitting, Damon had a worst case in mind: losing one year of income (he put it around $200,000 in salary). His wife worked full-time, and after eight years at Cisco the family had enough savings to cover it.
- He promised his wife a goal: hit $100,000 ARR by the end of 2021, and if he could not, he would go back to a tech job. He says he made it before 2021 ended.
- He tweeted publicly that if Testimonial hit $1,000 MRR he would quit his job. He reached $1,000 MRR at the end of March 2021 and quit because he had promised the internet.
- About a month later he reached $2,000 MRR. Early signs like $1,000 and $2,000 MRR also gave his wife more confidence, since she was carrying the family's income.
- His framing: it is a balance between freedom and financial stability. Staying employed gave stability. Quitting gave freedom, meaning time with his young daughter and no daily progress updates to a boss, which he called "a mental torture" after eight years. Quitting meant it would take time to rebuild financial stability.
- He felt that the job had become boring and full of trivial tasks.

chunks.heading: Building in public
chunks.text:
- Damon says his build-in-public journey started by accident. Because the first thing he launched was a community, he had to be its champion, posting videos and bringing people in from outside, so he restarted Twitter.
- He had signed up for Twitter when he moved to the US for his graduate degree but never used it. He says he had to become "an extrovert" and keep posting product updates.
- He wrote a thread summarizing what he shipped in 2020: most apps made $0, and only one made several thousand dollars within a few days. His point was "keep building and be patient."
- He shares almost everything publicly. His one exception is a private Slack group called 5k Twitter, for founders with several thousand followers on the way to 5,000.

chunks.heading: Why he took money from Calm Fund instead of traditional VC
chunks.text:
- Damon took money from Calm Fund (Tyler Tringas) in May 2021, after quitting in March. Calm Fund's Gil reached out to him on Twitter when he hit about $2,000 MRR, then he spoke with Tyler.
- His awareness of VC was limited to TechCrunch and Y Combinator. He applied to Y Combinator several times and never got an interview request.
- He heard Tyler on an Indie Hackers podcast and realized there was a VC that gives you money to keep doing what you already do, without pressure to move faster.
- He says traditional VCs, including Y Combinator, often do not consider solo founders. Calm Fund does not penalize solo founders or side projects.
- His fit criteria: he has family and a young child, so he did not want to take money that added external pressure.
- His view: "the biggest pressure should not be external." The founder should have their own motivation to grow. Money cannot solve the growth problem; the founder has to.
- Community was the other reason. As a solo founder who had just quit, he wanted a community of founders a few miles ahead of him with a couple of million dollars in ARR, who could give practical advice and inspire him. He did not want a community of CEOs of NASDAQ-listed public companies.
- He treats Calm Fund as a hands-off investor: he took the money and did not need supervision, but values having a community to lean on during lows.

chunks.heading: Advice for side-project founders deciding whether to go full time on funding
chunks.text:
- Figure out exactly what blocks you from quitting.
- If it is money, such as needing tens of thousands as a financial cushion, take the money. He says that makes the move nearly risk-free and opens a bigger opportunity to make an impact on your life and family.
- If it is confidence in the product, wait until you see initial product-market fit. Then, if you want faster growth, take money to fuel the business.
- He says he was well prepared before quitting: financial support and mental support from his wife, plus savings, plus a community of indie hacker founders to follow, which is why he took the funding from Calm Fund.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen recounts leaving Cisco after four failed side projects to build Testimonial to $800K+ ARR alone, then PDF.ai to $500K+. The free portion covers launching on Product Hunt, product-led growth loops, an affiliate program, buying a typo domain, and negotiating the risk with his wife. The PDF.ai growth channels are paywalled.

chunks.heading: Early path: unpaid leave, failed projects, and Testimonial's launch
chunks.text:
- Damon spent 8 years as a self-described "mediocre" engineer at Cisco. When COVID hit he was working from home with his wife and a 1-year-old, and he asked for 6 months of unpaid leave to spend time with his child.
- During that leave he built 5 side projects. The first was Indielog (indielog.com), a community where indie makers could vlog and share their journey. Three more projects failed and made no money, so four projects in a row earned $0 over about 6 months.
- The 5th project was Testimonial, a platform for business owners to collect video testimonials. It reused about 80% of the Indielog code. He added a landing page and Stripe payments and launched on Product Hunt at the end of his leave.
- Lesson he lived: reuse existing code and ship a thin, monetized version fast, rather than starting from scratch on each idea.

chunks.heading: Launch pricing and first revenue
chunks.text:
- At the Product Hunt launch he sold lifetime access to Testimonial for $199.
- He sold 30 lifetime deals and made $6K in the first two weeks. After four projects with $0 revenue, this was the first proof of demand.
- He moved to subscription pricing shortly afterward.
- Early customers came from the Indie Hackers community (he had met makers through indiehackers.com and indielog.com) and from social media. He tweeted that he was close to $1,000 MRR, and Andrew Gazdecki (founder of acquire.com) saw it and signed up for the highest plan.

chunks.heading: Quitting the job: validation threshold and deal with his spouse
chunks.text:
- He went back to Cisco after the leave, got staffed on a new project, and kept building Testimonial on nights and weekends.
- Four months later it made $2K MRR. He acknowledges that is not much in the Bay Area, but it was enough traction to try going full time.
- Quitting would cut household income by 50% and mean dipping into savings. He and his wife set explicit conditions:
  - He would go back to a tech job if he could not reach $100K ARR within a year.
  - She would cover the mortgage and bills in the meantime.
- Takeaway: he turned a risky decision into a time-boxed experiment with a clear revenue target and a fallback.

chunks.heading: Working routine as a solo founder with young kids
chunks.text:
- Kids were at home, so he split the day around their schedule:
  - Daytime: short breaks for bug fixes and answering support tickets.
  - Night: building new features after the kids went to bed (they napped and slept early).
- He even answered support tickets from his phone at the playground.
- Support and bug fixing stayed in the daytime gaps; deep feature work was reserved for uninterrupted night hours.

chunks.heading: Growing Testimonial to $800K+ ARR: product-led growth
chunks.text:
- Damon describes himself as an engineer who doesn't know much about marketing or sales, so he leaned on product-led growth.
- The core growth loop:
  1. A customer asks their own customers for testimonials.
  2. Testimonials appear on a "wall of love" landing page that carries the Testimonial logo.
  3. Visitors to the wall of love sign up for their own Testimonial account.
- The logo also pushes upgrades, because people pay for the paid plan to remove it.
- He hired his first employee at $400K ARR, to help with marketing, and says he's proud of scaling to mid-six figures by himself.

chunks.heading: Growth levers with outsized impact: affiliates and the .io domain
chunks.text:
- **Affiliate program:** anyone who signs up a paid customer earns 30% commission every month, and the referred customer gets 15% off for the first year. It contributes about 10-15% of Testimonial's total revenue.
- **Buying testimonials.io:** he noticed many people mistakenly visited testimonial.io instead of testimonial.to. He spent $35,000 to buy the .io domain. When he checked recently, that domain had brought in $80K in lifetime revenue, so he judged it worth the investment.

chunks.heading: PDF.ai: spun out of Testimonial
chunks.text:
- Damon says he had no interest in building another AI tool. The idea came from Testimonial customers, many of them e-commerce merchants who wanted a better testimonial collection rate.
- Their problem: merchants' customers often didn't know how to use the product, which led to negative reviews.
- His idea was a chatbot that lets a merchant's customers interact with product user manuals, which usually come as PDFs.
- PDF.ai grew to $500K+ ARR in a few months and, with Testimonial, brought his total to $1.3M+ ARR, all bootstrapped by himself. The channel breakdown for PDF.ai is behind the paywall in this source.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains how he bought a weekend-built AI project, rebranded it to PDF.ai, validated demand with a $99 lifetime deal, and grew it mostly through organic search thanks to an exact-match domain. He also shares what he would do differently: influencer marketing and partnerships.

chunks.heading: How Damon acquired PDF.ai and what it became
chunks.text:
- Damon was a software engineer at Cisco who began side hustling during Covid to build his own business. He also founded Testimonial, a platform for collecting and managing testimonials.
- He acquired PDF.ai (originally looseleaf.ai) from its founder, Josh, in May 2023, and grew it beyond $50K MRR.
- The original MVP was a weekend project: chat with one PDF at a time, no monetization. Its announcement on social media created hype, which he treats as a form of validation.
- The listing for sale caught his attention, and he bought it.
- Although he is a programmer by day job, the web app stack was new to him. He self-taught frontend and backend skills from Udemy.

chunks.heading: Launch playbook: rebrand plus a $99 lifetime deal
chunks.text:
- His "launch" was a rebrand to PDF.ai combined with adding monetization.
- To test whether anyone would pay, he offered a lifetime deal at $99.
- The first customer came within 24 hours of launching the LTD.
- The campaign ran 3 months and drew over 300 adopters.
- He says this gave enough validation for monetization plus strong financial support to invest in growth.
- He used the LTD revenue to hire a full-time engineer to work on the product.

chunks.heading: Domain name as the main marketing channel
chunks.text:
- Damon's top marketing effort is the relevant domain name.
- The domain tells Google explicitly what the product does, and the product is exactly what the domain says.
- Most traffic is organic, from people searching "PDF AI", and PDF.ai ranks at the top.
- His takeaway: a good, relevant domain gives a head start on competing for difficult keywords.

chunks.heading: Tool stack for running the business
chunks.text:
- OpenAI for the AI features
- Vercel for web hosting
- Deel to manage global pay for remote employees and contractors
- Mercury for banking
- Stripe for payments

chunks.heading: What Damon would do differently
chunks.text:
- He describes his growth so far as the very traditional route: keep building features, share updates publicly on social media, and wait for virality "like hitting a jackpot".
- He would explore more marketing channels.
- He would collaborate with influencers in their respective spaces, citing Jenni AI's TikTok marketing with various influencers as "quite ingenious" for rapidly increasing brand awareness.
- He would set up more partnerships with companies in related industries.
- He would do outreach to help older, legacy industries adopt AI technologies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Damon Chen explains how he built IndieLog (a vlog community for indie hackers) to solve his own remote-work isolation, and how a launch on Indie Hackers then Product Hunt plus daily presence seeded it. He also covers features designed to drive member activity and his plan to add gamification.

chunks.heading: Origin of IndieLog (formerly Lonely Dev) and the problem it solves
chunks.text:
Damon Chen is a software engineer at a Silicon Valley tech company and an indie hacker. He joined the Indie Hackers community several months before this interview and built two products: IndieLog and Backlogs.

- IndieLog is a video community where indie hackers vlog their startup journey together.
- Backlogs is a tool for collecting user feedback in one place. He built it while building IndieLog, after receiving feedback scattered across many channels.
- IndieLog came from his own problem. From March, lockdown meant working from home with less contact with others, and he wanted a channel to express himself.
- He first considered a YouTube channel but rejected it: "why do I have to expose myself to such a big audience? I don't want to be an influencer."
- He saw Indie Hackers posts about loneliness, remote happy hours and virtual meetups. That suggested a small "sub-YouTube" community made up only of indie hackers, gathering to talk about their work and day.

chunks.heading: Positioning: a human, video-only alternative to text forums
chunks.text:
- Damon notes that text forums like dev.to, indiehackers.com and some subreddits already exist and are "great", and he did not want to create another one.
- IndieLog is focused only on video. The goal is "something a little more human where people can have more personalized interactions."
- With video, people see each other and feel emotions, and members can build real relationships.
- A 2-minute limit on IndieLog videos keeps updates short. Longer content belongs on YouTube.

chunks.heading: Launch and early traction
chunks.text:
- He launched IndieLog on the Indiehackers community. One day later he had several new video uploads, which is where it began.
- Several weeks later he posted on Product Hunt, which also brought a lot of traffic.
- After that he did little promotion. He tried to be consistent: updating his own work on IndieLog almost every day and staying very active interacting with other members.
- At the time of the interview the community had fewer than 200 members. He viewed small as a plus: "It's like a friend circle I created all around the world", where he sees members' updates every day.

chunks.heading: Features built to drive member activity
chunks.text:
Damon's stated common goal for all features was to motivate members to post more video updates.

- **Topics:** a new topic every few weeks so all members talk about the same thing together. It gives new members a way to start when they want to say something but don't know where to begin.
- **Products:** a place to list the products members are working on. It helps members keep updating progress on a product, and videos link to each product's page, so the page shows all relevant videos.
- **IndieTuber:** a place for members to list their YouTube channels. Many indies also post longer videos on YouTube, so this promotes their channels given IndieLog's 2-minute limit.

chunks.heading: Future plans: retention through gamification and weekly check-ins
chunks.text:
- Focus more on promoting the community.
- Add weekly check-ins so people constantly update their progress.
- Add more gamification, such as challenging members to post an update every week. Members who manage 50 consecutive weeks in a year could earn stickers or other perks. He said he would see how much capacity he had for it.
- He was candid about marketing: "I'm not a marketing expert, lots of things I need to learn from the beginning."

At yesterday's meetup I asked Marc why he's never shipped an AI wrapper 😅

His two most profitable products have almost nothing to do with AI. Everyone else is chasing the AI hype. He just doesn't.

His answer had two parts.

1. he builds things he wants to use himself every day.

2. he asks what still won't be replaceable by AI in 5 or 10 years. His example was TrustMRR. Real buyers and real sellers who trust the place. An AI wrapper can die the day OpenAI ships one new feature. But nobody ships a feature that takes your buyers and sellers away.

So you pick the niche, and you don't chase whatever is hot this month. With AI there's a new hype almost every single month. You pick, and then you wait. The compounding only shows up years later. And if you don't actually love the thing, you won't stay long enough to see it.

There's a word going around in China right now, OPC, one person company. Everyone wants to build one, and with AI making everything fast and easy, everyone wants one that prints money fast.

Marc told us he wanted to build a social network early on, right after watching The Social Network. He wanted to get rich. Everyone starts there 🤪

We're both just normal people, zero followers, zero products, no idea how to get users. Honestly we still think about that last part every day.

If you're starting one of these, pick something you like and are already a bit good at. Ship one feature in your MVP. See if anyone wants it. If they do, stay on it and listen to the people using it.

Then go tell the story yourself and build your own flywheel.
